From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

## Executive view

The Seller package departs materially from the Buyer playbook. It compresses liability, expands deemed disclosure and Buyer knowledge, weakens key Completion protections, and attempts to place Title, Tax, IP, covenant and indemnity claims inside the general warranty regime.

The Seller’s characterisations of positions as “negotiated”, “agreed”, “settled” or “adequate” are not evidence of Buyer approval. In particular, there is no Amelia Frost written authority to accept either the 20% cap or the 18-month claims period.

## Material departures and proposed pushback

### 1. General warranty cap — reject 20%

**Seller position:** 20% of price / AUD 4.8 million.

**Playbook:** Start at 25% / AUD 6 million. A 20% cap is available only with Amelia Frost’s prior written authority identifying the draft; none has been given.

**Pushback:**

- Restore the general Warranty Claim cap to **AUD 6 million**.
- Do not treat the numerical match to the conditional fallback as approval.
- Make clear the general cap does not govern Fundamental/Title Claims, fraud, specific indemnities, Tax Claims, payment obligations or covenant claims unless separately and expressly agreed.

### 2. Thresholds — substantially too seller-friendly

**Seller position:**

- AUD 25,000 de minimis;
- AUD 250,000 basket;
- only the excess over the basket is recoverable.

**Playbook:**

- AUD 5,000 de minimis;
- AUD 50,000 aggregate basket;
- recovery from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded.

The Seller’s proposal increases both thresholds fivefold and changes the basket from a tipping basket to a deductible.

**Pushback:** Reinstate **AUD 5,000 / AUD 50,000 / first-dollar recovery**. Prevent related claims or a series of claims arising from the same facts from being artificially split for de minimis purposes.

### 3. General claims period — reject 18 months

**Seller position:** 18 months after Completion.

**Playbook:** 24 months. Eighteen months requires Amelia Frost’s prior written approval, which has not been given.

**Pushback:** Restore **24 months**. Ensure timely notice preserves the claim and that notice requirements do not demand final quantification before the relevant facts are known.

### 4. Fundamental and Title Claims — unacceptable general-regime treatment

**Seller position:** Capacity and title warranties subject to the same cap and time limit as general warranties “for administrative simplicity”.

**Playbook:** Separate regime, **100% cap**, at least **six years**, and no general basket, de minimis or knowledge bar.

A defect in ownership or authority goes to whether the Buyer receives the asset it is paying AUD 24 million for. Administrative convenience does not justify limiting that risk to AUD 4.8 million for 18 months.

**Pushback:**

- 100% of the purchase price cap;
- at least six years;
- outside the general de minimis and basket;
- no Buyer-knowledge or disclosure defence for title, ownership, capacity or authority;
- cover ownership, valid issuance, absence of encumbrances, power and authority, and valid transfer of all shares.

### 5. “All Claims” override — reject

**Seller position:** General limitations apply to all Claims unless expressly excluded; limitations, exclusive remedies and non-reliance apply to Claims “of any nature”.

This risks silently sweeping Title, Tax, IP, specific indemnities, payment obligations and covenant breaches into the general cap and time bar.

**Pushback:** Use separate, affirmative regimes. General Warranty Claim limitations should apply **only** to defined General Warranty Claims. Expressly exclude:

- Fundamental and Title Claims;
- Tax Claims;
- specific indemnities, including Ironquay;
- Completion payment and adjustment obligations;
- covenant and undertaking claims;
- equitable relief and specific performance;
- fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct.

Tax and IP terms remain open; the Seller cannot declare them “settled” under the general regime. The Buyer should not assume that either category is unlimited, but neither should be conceded into the general regime without a substantive resolution.

### 6. Fraud and deliberate wrongdoing — mandatory carve-out

The Seller’s proposed all-Claims limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance language would apparently extend to fraud and other deliberate wrongdoing. That is contrary to the playbook.

**Pushback:** Add an express carve-out, to the maximum extent enforceable, for:

- fraud;
- wilful concealment; and
- deliberate misconduct.

The carve-out must apply across caps, thresholds, baskets, time limits, exclusive-remedy provisions, non-reliance language and any other contractual limitation. This is non-waivable under the Buyer mandate.

### 7. Disclosure standard — reject general data-room and public-register disclosure

**Seller position:** Every matter contained or referred to anywhere in the data room, accounts, statutory registers and public records is deemed disclosed.

**Playbook:** Only specific fair disclosure; no whole-data-room, public-register or prudent-search deemed disclosure.

The general disclosure transfers the burden to the Buyer to infer exceptions and legal consequences across the entire diligence record. A document’s presence does not necessarily fairly disclose the nature and scope of the matter qualifying a particular warranty.

**Pushback:**

- Delete paragraphs 1.1 and 1.2 as general warranty qualifications.
- Require each qualification to identify:
  - the specific warranty affected;
  - the relevant facts and circumstances;
  - their nature and reasonably ascertainable scope; and
  - precise document references.
- Public availability or data-room access alone must not amount to disclosure.
- The data-room snapshot is stated to be as at **22 September 2026**. Require a refreshed index, export and seller confirmation of all additions, removals and changes through signing/Completion.

Paragraph 1.4’s refusal to admit liability is not itself objectionable, but it cannot cure inadequate disclosure or determine whether the facts constitute a breach.

### 8. Buyer knowledge — delete the blanket exclusion

**Seller position:** No claim for anything known by the Buyer or its advisers, including anything discoverable from the data room or public records.

This is broader than actual knowledge and effectively imports constructive knowledge, adviser knowledge and a prudent-search obligation.

**Pushback:**

- Delete the blanket exclusion.
- If any knowledge limitation is ultimately considered, it should be narrowly defined and not based on matters that were merely discoverable.
- Seller warranty knowledge qualifiers should instead use named Seller knowledge persons and reasonable enquiry.
- No knowledge defence may apply to title, capacity, authority, fraud or a specific indemnity.

### 9. Bluefen consent — unresolved material Completion risk

Bluefen represents approximately AUD 3.6 million of FY26 revenue, around 30%. The Disclosure Letter confirms:

- no final written consent is included; and
- no evidence shows the associated conditions have been satisfied.

“Reasonable endeavours” is inadequate for a material customer consent. Treating the condition as satisfied merely when a letter is delivered could leave underlying conditions outstanding or the consent ineffective.

**Pushback:** Make Completion conditional on:

- effective written Bluefen consent in an agreed form;
- satisfaction or valid waiver of all conditions attached to it;
- evidence satisfactory to the Buyer; and
- no adverse amendment, fee, termination right or other condition without Buyer approval.

Delivery alone must not deem the condition satisfied. Any waiver of this condition should require express Buyer agreement.

### 10. Riverlark debt and security — must be dealt with at Completion

The Disclosure Letter confirms approximately AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding and no final security discharge is available. This is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free transaction if left outstanding.

**Pushback:**

- Obtain a current payout letter immediately before Completion.
- Pay Riverlark directly from Completion funds.
- Obtain effective releases and discharges of all Company security at Completion.
- Reflect repayment clearly in the Completion statement and funds flow.

A release “following Completion” is not acceptable. The playbook permits consideration of a post-Completion release only with an irrevocable undertaking and Amelia Frost’s approval; no such approval exists.

### 11. Employee bonuses — funds flow omission must be corrected

DD-005 records AUD 420,000 of Completion bonuses, while the funds flow omits them. Payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs have not been established.

The statement that the bonuses are “a matter for the Seller” is insufficient unless the documents and funds flow actually ensure that economic result.

**Pushback:**

- Itemise the AUD 420,000 and all triggered on-costs in the Completion statement/funds flow; or
- require the Seller to fund and discharge them separately, without recourse to Company cash or post-Completion Buyer funds.
- Obtain calculations for payroll tax, superannuation, leave effects and other on-costs.
- Include protection against duplicate payment or post-Completion Company liability.

The debt-free/cash-free mechanics must not silently leave these liabilities with the acquired Company.

### 12. Ironquay IP — narrow indemnity and unverified cure are inadequate

The documents indicate that transfer of SOW3 Project Materials depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. The AUD 180,000 figure is only an internal record; there is no independent verification of the outstanding amount, receipt or confirmatory assignment.

**Pushback:**

- Preserve the SOW3 payment cure, but verify the current payout directly.
- Require cleared payment and written confirmation that all relevant IP has transferred.
- Obtain confirmatory assignments and releases where appropriate.
- Broaden the indemnity beyond the single stated payment to cover losses arising from:
  - failure to obtain ownership or valid rights in the Project Materials;
  - unpaid fees or related claims;
  - infringement or third-party ownership assertions associated with the matter; and
  - costs of cure, replacement and enforcement.
- Keep the specific indemnity outside the general warranty basket, de minimis and knowledge defence, with its separate cap and duration to remain expressly negotiated.

The Buyer should not accept AUD 180,000 as verified in either direction.

### 13. Export/privacy incident — preserve and investigate without overstatement

The disclosure is appropriately cautious in some respects: it does not establish access, exact scope, notification obligations, confirmed breach, harm or loss. The Buyer should not convert preliminary facts into an assumed breach or an arbitrary price demand.

However, describing the matter as “not expected to be material” is an unverified Seller conclusion.

**Pushback:**

- Require preservation of logs, messages, export records and forensic evidence.
- Require a properly scoped investigation and regular written updates.
- Require prompt notice of any evidence of access, dissemination, affected records, legal notification duty or regulator/customer contact.
- Prevent deletion, alteration or avoidable remediation without consultation.
- Preserve warranty and indemnity rights pending the investigation.

Any remediation, notification or specific indemnity should be based on verified findings, not the Seller’s preliminary materiality assessment.

### 14. Sandbar renewals — investigate; do not automatically deduct

The Seller calls the AUD 330,000 renewals ordinary-course costs, but the Disclosure Letter does not establish whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.

**Pushback:**

- Obtain the three contracts, renewal dates, termination rights, service periods, invoicing and approval history.
- Determine whether the renewals relate to pre- or post-Completion benefit and whether any amount is accrued.
- Test compliance with interim operating covenants and agreed budgeting.

Do **not** automatically classify the AUD 330,000 as Debt or deduct it from price. Treatment should follow the verified contract terms and agreed price definitions.

### 15. Title evidence — DD-012 is not independent proof

The internal share register is relevant evidence, but it is not independently conclusive proof of legal and beneficial ownership, valid issuance, absence of encumbrances or authority to transfer.

**Pushback:** Require a separate title package, including:

- original or replacement share certificate evidence;
- incorporation and ASIC searches;
- constitution and relevant shareholder/director approvals;
- historic issue and transfer records;
- PPSR and other applicable encumbrance searches;
- confirmation of no options, convertibles, trusts, nominees or third-party interests;
- executed transfer instruments and updated registers at Completion.

The Seller should warrant title independently of what DD-012 records.

### 16. Office lease and Mossvale — do not manufacture consent requirements

The specific disclosures say the office lease involves a notification obligation, not necessarily consent, and that the Mossvale assignment restriction does not on its face apply merely to a share sale.

The Buyer should verify the complete clauses and related definitions, but should not automatically insist on consent or a price deduction without a contractual basis. If notice is required, require timely evidence of compliance.

## Recommended negotiation position

1. Reinstate the Buyer’s core liability package: **25% cap, AUD 5,000 de minimis, AUD 50,000 tipping basket and 24 months**.
2. Establish a separate Fundamental/Title regime: **100% cap, at least six years, no thresholds or knowledge defence**.
3. Add the mandatory fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct carve-out across every limitation and reliance provision.
4. Reject general data-room/public-record disclosure and constructive Buyer knowledge.
5. Make effective Bluefen consent, including satisfaction of its conditions, a genuine Completion condition.
6. Repay Riverlark directly from Completion funds and obtain effective security releases at Completion.
7. Itemise or seller-fund the AUD 420,000 bonuses and all applicable on-costs.
8. Verify and cure the Ironquay position, obtain IP transfer evidence and broaden the specific indemnity.
9. Preserve evidence and complete the DD-006 investigation without assuming a confirmed breach or loss.
10. Investigate Sandbar before deciding treatment; make no automatic Debt classification.
11. Keep Title, Tax, IP, specific indemnities, payments and covenants out of any hidden “all Claims” general-regime override.
12. Require independent title and encumbrance evidence rather than relying solely on DD-012.
13. Refresh the diligence and disclosure record from the 22 September 2026 cutoff through signing and Completion.
14. Treat Tax and IP as open items—not settled—and reserve the Buyer’s position pending full drafting.

The Buyer should not accept AUD 180,000 as verified in either direction.

### 13. Export/privacy incident — preserve and investigate without overstatement

The disclosure is appropriately cautious in some respects: it does not establish access, exact scope, notification obligations, confirmed breach, harm or loss. The Buyer should not convert preliminary facts into an assumed breach or an arbitrary price demand.

However, describing the matter as “not expected to be material” is an unverified Seller conclusion.

**Pushback:**

- Require preservation of logs, messages, export records and forensic evidence.
- Require a properly scoped investigation and regular written updates.
- Require prompt notice of any evidence of access, dissemination, affected records, legal notification duty or regulator/customer contact.
- Prevent deletion, alteration or avoidable remediation without consultation.
- Preserve warranty and indemnity rights pending the investigation.

Any remediation, notification or specific indemnity should be based on verified findings, not the Seller’s preliminary materiality assessment.

### 14. Sandbar renewals — investigate; do not automatically deduct

The Seller calls the AUD 330,000 renewals ordinary-course costs, but the Disclosure Letter does not establish whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.

**Pushback:**

- Obtain the three contracts, renewal dates, termination rights, service periods, invoicing and approval history.
- Determine whether the renewals relate to pre- or post-Completion benefit and whether any amount is accrued.
- Test compliance with interim operating covenants and agreed budgeting.

Do **not** automatically classify the AUD 330,000 as Debt or deduct it from price. Treatment should follow the verified contract terms and agreed price definitions.

### 15. Title evidence — DD-012 is not independent proof

The internal share register is relevant evidence, but it is not independently conclusive proof of legal and beneficial ownership, valid issuance, absence of encumbrances or authority to transfer.

**Pushback:** Require a separate title package, including:

- original or replacement share certificate evidence;
- incorporation and ASIC searches;
- constitution and relevant shareholder/director approvals;
- historic issue and transfer records;
- PPSR and other applicable encumbrance searches;
- confirmation of no options, convertibles, trusts, nominees or third-party interests;
- executed transfer instruments and updated registers at Completion.

The Seller should warrant title independently of what DD-012 records.

### 16. Office lease and Mossvale — do not manufacture consent requirements

The specific disclosures say the office lease involves a notification obligation, not necessarily consent, and that the Mossvale assignment restriction does not on its face apply merely to a share sale.

The Buyer should verify the complete clauses and related definitions, but should not automatically insist on consent or a price deduction without a contractual basis. If notice is required, require timely evidence of compliance.
